note: Curated videos for video-library.html, watch.html?v=<slug> and <figure data-video="<slug>"> in lessons. Hand-edited; validate with npm run check:videos. Times are positions in the source video ("1:30"); start/end make a clip; pauses stop the video and show the question. Allowed sources: assets/js/video-sources.mjs.

groups.title: Science & Wonder
groups.sub: Cosmos, scale, and the patterns of nature

groups.title: Technology
groups.sub: How systems work and myths get busted

groups.title: Purpose & Voice
groups.sub: Resilience, creativity, and thinking for yourself

groups.title: Film & Animation
groups.sub: How pictures learned to move, and then to talk

pale-blue-dot.title: Carl Sagan — Pale Blue Dot
pale-blue-dot.desc: Carl Sagan reflects on Earth seen from 3.7 billion miles away and what that perspective asks of us.
pale-blue-dot.insight: Use scale to deepen humility. Ask how scientific imagery can change ethical choices.

powers-of-ten.title: Powers of Ten (1977)
powers-of-ten.desc: The Eames Office film travels from a Chicago picnic to cosmic scale, then inward toward the atom.
powers-of-ten.insight: Build intuition for exponents and scientific notation. Pause to predict what the next power of ten will reveal.

nature-by-numbers.title: Nature by Numbers — 4K Remastered
nature-by-numbers.desc: An artist-made exploration of Fibonacci numbers, the golden ratio, and geometric patterns in living forms.
nature-by-numbers.insight: Treat the film as a mathematical claim, not proof. Ask students where the model fits nature and where it simplifies it.

what-is-the-internet.title: What Is the Internet?
what-is-the-internet.desc: A short introduction to the connected systems and shared protocols behind the internet.
what-is-the-internet.insight: Help students distinguish the internet from the web and identify the physical systems beneath a browser page.

jobs-on-failure.title: Steve Jobs on Failure
jobs-on-failure.desc: An archival interview excerpt about failure, iteration, and continuing to build.
jobs-on-failure.insight: Connect setbacks to revision. Ask what evidence would distinguish perseverance from repeating the same mistake.

pauses.ask: Why does Jobs say that a willingness to ask for help and risk failure is what separates people who build things from people who only dream?

jobs-secrets-of-life.title: Steve Jobs — Secrets of Life
jobs-secrets-of-life.desc: An archival interview excerpt about questioning assumptions and making useful things.
jobs-secrets-of-life.insight: Listen critically: which ideas are actionable, and which depend on privilege, context, or hindsight?

pauses.ask: Jobs says life becomes much broader once you realize who built everything around you. What does he mean?

jobs-2005-stanford-commencement.title: Steve Jobs' 2005 Stanford Commencement Address
jobs-2005-stanford-commencement.desc: Steve Jobs delivers his landmark 2005 Stanford address on connecting the dots, love and loss, and staying hungry and foolish.
jobs-2005-stanford-commencement.insight: Connect Jobs's calligraphy class and NeXT/Pixar detour to the lesson's themes of design and resilience.

chapters.label: Remembering you are going to die

pauses.ask: How did dropping out and auditing a calligraphy class end up directly shaping the Macintosh ten years later?
Jobs says getting fired from Apple was 'the best thing that could have happened.' What creative freedom did it give him?

apollo-15-hammer-feather.title: Apollo 15 — The Hammer and the Feather (1971)
apollo-15-hammer-feather.desc: Standing on the Moon, Commander David Scott drops a geologic hammer and a falcon feather at the same moment to test Galileo's claim about falling bodies.
apollo-15-hammer-feather.insight: Get a prediction from every student before the drop. Then ask what air does on Earth that the Moon takes away, and what the same drop would look like inside a vacuum chamber here.

pauses.ask: Scott is about to let go of both at once. Predict: which one hits the ground first, and why?

apollo-11-eagle-has-landed.title: The Eagle Has Landed: The Flight of Apollo 11 (1969)
apollo-11-eagle-has-landed.desc: NASA's 1969 film of the first crewed Moon landing, cut to the powered descent, touchdown and first moonwalk, shot on 16 mm film from the lunar module window.
apollo-11-eagle-has-landed.insight: Pair it with the guidance-computer section: this descent is when the 1202 alarms and the fuel limit were real. Ask what the crew trusted the computer to do, and what Armstrong took back by hand.

pauses.ask: The computer was steering Eagle into a boulder field, so Armstrong is flying the last stretch by hand. What does he need to see and know, and how fast does he have to decide?

trip-to-the-moon-1902.title: A Trip to the Moon (Georges Méliès, 1902)
trip-to-the-moon-1902.desc: The silent fantasy that imagined a Moon voyage 67 years before Apollo: a capsule fired from a giant cannon straight into the eye of the Man in the Moon.
trip-to-the-moon-1902.insight: Set imagination against engineering. List what Méliès got wrong (a cannon launch, a Moon you can breathe on) and what he got right (a capsule, a crew, a splashdown at sea).

pauses.ask: Méliès fires his explorers out of a cannon. What would a launch like that do to the people inside, and how did Apollo solve the same problem?

earthrise-apollo-8.title: Earthrise: The 45th Anniversary
earthrise-apollo-8.desc: Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter data and the Apollo 8 crew's own onboard audio recreate December 24, 1968, when Bill Anders photographed Earth rising over the Moon.
earthrise-apollo-8.insight: Listen for the scramble to find color film. Ask why one photograph of our own planet mattered more to the crew than anything they found at the Moon.

jupiter-great-red-spot.title: Jupiter's Great Red Spot Shrinks and Grows
jupiter-great-red-spot.desc: Decades of Hubble and spacecraft images show the Great Red Spot shrinking in area while growing taller, with its winds holding steady.
jupiter-great-red-spot.insight: A storm wider than Earth that has lasted for centuries: ask what keeps it going with no land to slow it down, and why a shrinking storm might stretch upward instead of spinning faster.

sdo-sunspot-two-weeks.title: Two Weeks in the Life of a Sunspot
sdo-sunspot-two-weeks.desc: NASA's Solar Dynamics Observatory follows one sunspot group from July 5 to 17, 2017, as it grows and is carried across the face of the Sun.
sdo-sunspot-two-weeks.insight: The spot travels because the Sun turns. It crosses half the disk in about two weeks, so ask students to estimate how long one full rotation takes (about 27 days, seen from Earth).

perpetual-ocean.title: Perpetual Ocean
perpetual-ocean.desc: Surface currents of the world ocean from June 2005 to December 2007, drawn from NASA/MIT/JPL ocean-model data: the Gulf Stream, the great gyres and thousands of eddies.
perpetual-ocean.insight: Find a current carrying warm water toward the poles and one carrying cold water toward the equator. Then ask which zones feel these currents, and which never do.
perpetual-ocean.rights: Public domain — NASA Goddard Space Flight Center

global-temperature-1880-2025.title: Global Temperature Anomalies, 1880–2025
global-temperature-1880-2025.channel: NASA Scientific Visualization Studio · NASA GISS
global-temperature-1880-2025.desc: NASA's map of how much warmer or cooler each place ran than its 1951–1980 average, year by year from 1880 to 2025. The video has no sound.
global-temperature-1880-2025.insight: This is the measured record, not a model. Have students note when the map turns warm and stays warm, then compare that with where the simulator's scenarios begin.

pauses.ask: We're about halfway through the record. Has the map changed much yet? Predict what the last 30 seconds will look like.

hurricane-harvey-goes16.title: Hurricane Harvey from GOES-16 (2017)
hurricane-harvey-goes16.desc: NOAA's GOES-16 weather satellite watches Category 4 Hurricane Harvey come ashore near Rockport, Texas, on August 25, 2017.
hurricane-harvey-goes16.insight: Loop it a few times. Have students find the eye, the spiral rain bands and the direction of spin, then explain why hurricanes north of the equator turn counterclockwise.

mount-st-helens-1980.title: Eruption of Mount St. Helens (1980)
mount-st-helens-1980.desc: The U.S. Forest Service's film of May 18, 1980: the eruption column, the rescues, and the mudflows that choked rivers miles from the mountain.
mount-st-helens-1980.insight: Connect the simulator's controls to consequences. A collapsing flank released the gas pressure sideways, and melted snow and ice became the lahars. Ask which hazards reached people farthest from the summit.
mount-st-helens-1980.rights: Public domain — U.S. Forest Service film, National Archives (ARC 13364)

pauses.ask: The eruption happened miles upstream. Why are these rivers suddenly full of logs and mud?
The ash is about to spread east, not evenly in every direction. What decides where the ash falls?

tacoma-narrows-collapse.title: Tacoma Narrows Bridge Collapse (1940)
tacoma-narrows-collapse.channel: Internet Archive · stock footage, sound version
tacoma-narrows-collapse.desc: “Galloping Gertie” twists in a steady wind on November 7, 1940, until the center span tears loose and falls into the Narrows.
tacoma-narrows-collapse.insight: Push past “resonance” as a one-word answer. The twisting was aeroelastic flutter: the deck's own motion kept pulling energy out of the wind. Ask which design changes would break that feedback loop (a stiffer deck, open trusses, an aerodynamic shape).
tacoma-narrows-collapse.rights: Public domain — U.S. copyright not renewed (Internet Archive item SF121)

pauses.ask: The wind that morning was about 40 mph: strong, but no hurricane. How can a steady wind tear apart a steel bridge?

grace-hopper-nanoseconds.title: Grace Hopper Hands Out Nanoseconds (1982)
grace-hopper-nanoseconds.desc: From Captain Grace Hopper's 1982 NSA lecture: she explains a nanosecond by handing out 11.8-inch pieces of wire, the farthest a signal can travel in a billionth of a second.
grace-hopper-nanoseconds.insight: Hopper turns an invisible unit into something you can hold. Have students make their own: how long is a microsecond of wire, and how far does a signal get during one tick of a 3 GHz processor (about 10 cm)?
grace-hopper-nanoseconds.rights: Public domain — NSA (U.S. government work), digitized by the National Archives

pauses.ask: Light travels about 186,000 miles every second. Before she tells you: how long is a nanosecond of wire?
Why would Hopper want a microsecond of wire hanging over every programmer's desk?

ford-model-t-assembly-1919.title: Ford Model T Assembly Line (1919)
ford-model-t-assembly-1919.desc: Ford's own silent film of Model Ts being built station by station, with a title card for each step from body to engine to the drive off the line.
ford-model-t-assembly-1919.insight: Time one station and estimate cars per hour. Then weigh the trade-off: the line made a car affordable, so what did it cost the people doing one task all day?

pauses.ask: Count the workers at one station. What does each of them need to know, and what don't they need to know?

steamboat-willie-1928.title: Steamboat Willie (1928)
steamboat-willie-1928.channel: Walt Disney & Ub Iwerks · 16 mm print scan
steamboat-willie-1928.desc: Mickey Mouse's breakthrough, and one of the first cartoons with sound fully synchronized to the picture. Scanned from an original 16 mm print.
steamboat-willie-1928.insight: Every toot and whistle had to land on an exact frame. Ask how animators could time sound before they could hear it (Disney's team planned the music beat by beat on exposure sheets). Note: the later gags use animals as instruments, which is 1928 slapstick worth a quick discussion.
steamboat-willie-1928.rights: Public domain in the U.S. since 2024. Mickey Mouse is still a Disney trademark.

pauses.ask: Every whistle lines up with the picture. In 1928, how would animators know which frame each sound belongs on?

muybridge-galloping-horse.title: Muybridge's Galloping Horse (1887)
muybridge-galloping-horse.desc: Muybridge's sequential photographs of a galloping horse, played back as motion. They proved that all four hooves leave the ground at once.
muybridge-galloping-horse.insight: This is animation's ancestor: still frames shown fast enough turn into motion. Ask how many frames per second the eye needs, and compare that with the 24 frames per second of sound film.

wright-inventing-airplane.title: Inventing the Airplane, Changing the World
wright-inventing-airplane.channel: Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum
wright-inventing-airplane.desc: Grades 4–9 · A Smithsonian museum introduction to the Wright brothers’ invention and the significance of their four flights on December 17, 1903.
wright-inventing-airplane.insight: Before watching, name the three problems: lift, power, and control. Afterward, explain why a longer fourth flight offered more evidence than the first flight alone.
wright-inventing-airplane.rights: Smithsonian video; streamed from the official provider, not licensed for redistribution.

wright-first-flight-photo.title: The Story a Photo Tells — Wright Brothers’ First Flight
wright-first-flight-photo.channel: Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum
wright-first-flight-photo.desc: Grades 4–9 · Smithsonian STEM in 30 examines the famous first-flight photograph as a historical source. Pair it with the enlarged photograph in the Wright brothers lesson.
wright-first-flight-photo.insight: First write one observation, one inference, and one question about the photograph. After watching, revise an inference and name evidence the still image cannot supply.
wright-first-flight-photo.rights: Smithsonian video; streamed from the official provider, not licensed for redistribution.

moon-phases-libration.title: Moon Phase and Libration (2026)
moon-phases-libration.channel: NASA Scientific Visualization Studio · Ernie Wright
moon-phases-libration.desc: An hourly visualization of the Moon across an entire year based on Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter data, revealing the cycle of phases, the apparent wobble of libration, and shifting crater shadows.
moon-phases-libration.insight: Focus students on the limb of the Moon: notice that while the Moon is tidally locked to Earth, orbital eccentricity and axial tilt produce libration, letting us see 59% of the surface over time. Ask how sunlight angle changes our perception of crater depth.
moon-phases-libration.rights: Public domain — NASA (U.S. government work), SVS ID 5587

pauses.ask: The Moon always shows us roughly the same face, yet it appears to nod and rock. What orbital mechanics cause this libration?
Notice how crater rims pop into sharp relief only near the shadow line (the terminator). Why do craters near full Moon look flat?

orion-nebula-3d.title: Flight Through the Orion Nebula in 3D
orion-nebula-3d.channel: NASA SVS · Space Telescope Science Institute
orion-nebula-3d.desc: A scientific three-dimensional fly-through of the Great Nebula in Orion (M42) blending visible Hubble Space Telescope data with infrared Spitzer observations to pierce dense stellar birth clouds.
orion-nebula-3d.insight: Watch how switching from optical to infrared light changes the scene completely: cold interstellar dust that blocks visible light glows warmly in infrared, unmasking embryonic protostars and protoplanetary disks.
orion-nebula-3d.rights: Public domain — NASA / STScI (U.S. government work), SVS ID 12086

chapters.label: Crossing into infrared: piercing the veil

pauses.ask: Thick clouds of dust appear pitch black in visible light, but shine brightly when viewed in infrared. What does that tell us about the temperature and nature of the dust?

solar-flare-sdo.title: SDO — Extreme Ultraviolet Solar Flare
solar-flare-sdo.channel: NASA Goddard Space Flight Center · Solar Dynamics Observatory
solar-flare-sdo.desc: NASA's Solar Dynamics Observatory captures an intense mid-level solar flare on the sun's limb across multiple extreme ultraviolet wavelengths, revealing coronal magnetic loops snapping and releasing explosive energy.
solar-flare-sdo.insight: SDO color-codes ultraviolet wavelengths that human eyes cannot see. Ask students what holds plasma hotter than a million degrees in towering curved arches above the solar surface.
solar-flare-sdo.rights: Public domain — NASA (U.S. government work), GSFC 2016

chapters.label: Active magnetic region on the solar limb
The flare erupts across ultraviolet bands

pauses.ask: Watch the intense flash of ultraviolet light. Why do solar flares cause radio blackouts and satellite disruptions on Earth eight minutes later?

earth-at-night-black-marble.title: Earth at Night — The Black Marble
earth-at-night-black-marble.desc: A seamless rotating globe composite of Earth at night created from the Day-Night Band of the VIIRS sensor aboard the Suomi NPP satellite, mapping city lights, transportation arteries, and unlit wilderness.
earth-at-night-black-marble.insight: Trace the brightest ribbons of light across the continents: they outline coastlines, major navigable rivers (like the Nile), and rail networks. Ask what geographic features explain the sharp borders between brightly lit and pitch-dark regions.
earth-at-night-black-marble.rights: Public domain — NASA Goddard Space Flight Center / NOAA, SVS ID 30878

pauses.ask: Look closely at the Nile River winding through North Africa. Why do human populations and lights concentrate so sharply along narrow river valleys in arid regions?

communications-primer-1953.title: A Communications Primer (Charles & Ray Eames, 1953)
communications-primer-1953.channel: Charles & Ray Eames · IBM · Prelinger Archives
communications-primer-1953.desc: Charles and Ray Eames translate Claude Shannon's mathematical theory of communication into visual cinema: information sources, encoders, channels, noise, language redundancy, bits, and binary decisions.
communications-primer-1953.insight: This film connects telecommunications engineering to human cognition, design, and painting. Use it to introduce information theory: how bits represent decisions and how redundancy protects messages against noise.
communications-primer-1953.rights: Public domain — Prelinger Archives (U.S. copyright not renewed, published 1953)

chapters.label: The electronic calculator and punch cards

pauses.ask: The Eameses define noise as any outside force that alters the transmitted signal unpredictably. What counts as noise when you read a book or message a friend?
A choice between two possibilities gives one bit of information. How many bits are needed to choose among 16 possibilities, and why?
A printed photograph is made of half a million black or white decisions. How does breaking a complex image into binary dots compare to modern digital pixels?

trip-down-market-street-1906.title: A Trip Down Market Street (1906)
trip-down-market-street-1906.channel: Miles Brothers · Prelinger Archives 4K Film Scan
trip-down-market-street-1906.desc: A camera mounted on the front of a cable car captures San Francisco's Market Street bustling with pedestrians, horse carts, and early automobiles just four days before the 1906 earthquake and fire.
trip-down-market-street-1906.insight: Observe the transportation transition in motion: horse wagons, cable cars, electric trolleys, and motorcars all share the same unstriped street. Ask how people negotiated right-of-way before traffic lights, lane markings, or crosswalks.
trip-down-market-street-1906.rights: Public domain — published April 1906, copyright expired; preserved by Prelinger Archives

chapters.label: Passing 6th Street and Golden Gate Avenue
The Call Building and newspaper row

pauses.ask: Watch the pedestrians crossing directly in front of the cable car and horse carriages. How did street safety and right-of-way work before painted crosswalks and traffic signals?
Notice the tracks beneath the cable car. How did the underground cable propulsion system allow cars to climb hills and cruise wide streets without overhead wires or engines?

helen-keller-speech-1930.title: How Helen Keller Learned to Talk (1930)
helen-keller-speech-1930.desc: In this historic talking newsreel, teacher Anne Sullivan demonstrates the tactile method used to teach Helen Keller how to speak, feeling the physical vibrations of the throat, lips, and nose.
helen-keller-speech-1930.insight: Highlight the patience, sensory awareness, and mutual trust between Sullivan and Keller. Discuss how sensory input can be translated: when auditory and visual channels are unavailable, touch conveys rhythm, pitch, and phonetics.
helen-keller-speech-1930.rights: Public domain — newsreel published 1930 without copyright notice or renewal

chapters.label: Helen feels throat and lip vibrations
Helen Keller speaks aloud to the world

pauses.ask: Sullivan places Helen's hand on her larynx, lips, and nose. What physical properties of sound waves is Helen feeling that allow her to imitate spoken words?
Helen speaks her sentence: 'I am not dumb now.' Reflect on what finding a voice meant for her ability to advocate for others.

jfk-civil-rights-address-1963.title: John F. Kennedy — Address on Civil Rights (1963)
jfk-civil-rights-address-1963.channel: White House Communications Agency · National Archives
jfk-civil-rights-address-1963.desc: President John F. Kennedy's televised address to the American people on June 11, 1963, defining civil rights not merely as a legal issue or economic debate, but as an inescapable moral imperative.
jfk-civil-rights-address-1963.insight: Analyze Kennedy's rhetorical shift from enforcement of court orders to fundamental human ethics: 'It is not a sectional issue... Nor is this a partisan issue.' Discuss how defining a question as a moral duty alters the terms of civic debate.
jfk-civil-rights-address-1963.rights: Public domain — U.S. government official presidential address (June 11, 1963)

chapters.label: Events at the University of Alabama
A nation founded on the proposition of equality
Civil rights as a moral issue
The gap between American ideals and daily reality
A call for federal legislation and civic action

pauses.ask: Kennedy asks: 'Who among us would be content to have the color of his skin changed and stand in his place?' How does asking listeners to imagine themselves in another's shoes change an argument from law to conscience?
Kennedy argues that token changes cannot resolve fundamental injustice. What evidence does he offer to show that piecemeal remedies are insufficient?

gertie-the-dinosaur-1914.title: Gertie the Dinosaur (Winsor McCay, 1914)
gertie-the-dinosaur-1914.desc: The birth of character animation: cartoonist Winsor McCay hand-drew 10,000 frames on rice paper to give Gertie lifelike weight, playful stubbornness, emotional depth, and comedic personality.
gertie-the-dinosaur-1914.insight: Notice how McCay conveys weight, breathing, and inertia in Gertie's body: when she walks, the ground shakes; when she breathes, her ribs expand. Compare Gertie's personality-driven movement to earlier purely mechanical trick films.
gertie-the-dinosaur-1914.rights: Public domain — published 1914, copyright expired; preserved by the Library of Congress

chapters.label: A reluctant bow to the audience
Winsor McCay steps into the cartoon

pauses.ask: Look closely at Gertie's chest and belly as she stands still. How did McCay make an ink-drawn creature appear to breathe and have physical weight?
Gertie gets scolded and begins to cry before being cheered up with a pumpkin. Why was giving an animated character emotional vulnerability such a radical breakthrough in 1914?

serpentine-dance-1895.title: Annabelle Serpentine Dance (Edison / Dickson, 1895)
serpentine-dance-1895.desc: Dancer Annabelle Moore performs the serpentine dance for Edison's Kinetograph, hand-tinted frame by individual frame with luminous dyes to create swirling kinetic waves of changing color.
serpentine-dance-1895.insight: Before color film emulsions existed, women artisans at the Edison laboratory painted each 35mm celluloid frame under magnifying lenses. Ask students how color changes our experience of rhythm, volume, and bodily movement.

pauses.ask: Every single frame of this 1895 film was colored by hand with a tiny paintbrush. How does the changing color alter your perception of the fabric's three-dimensional shape?

lichtspiel-opus-1-1921.title: Lichtspiel: Opus I (Walther Ruttmann, 1921)
lichtspiel-opus-1-1921.desc: The very first public abstract film in cinema history: flowing hand-colored geometric forms, dynamic pulses, and organic wave shapes composed like visual symphonic music.
lichtspiel-opus-1-1921.insight: Ruttmann abandoned traditional characters and storylines to create 'an art of pure time and motion.' Ask students what emotions or physical sensations abstract shapes and tempos evoke without words or recognizable scenery.
lichtspiel-opus-1-1921.rights: Public domain — published 1921 in Germany, copyright expired

pauses.ask: Notice how the shapes seem to inhale, expand, and drift like living cells or sea creatures. Can purely abstract animation convey life and emotion without characters?
Ruttmann composed this film with a dedicated musical score by Max Butting. How does the tempo of motion on screen substitute for musical notes and counterpoint?
